Chapter 3. Methodology 16
3.1 Introduction
EduVerse combines multiple academic and administrative workflows that
share user roles, data, permissions, and interaction rules. Developing these
capabilities therefore required a methodology that could accommodate
progressive refinement while preserving consistency across the wider
platform.
Because dependencies between features often became clearer during
implementation and testing, the development process needed to support
repeated analysis, refinement, and integration rather than rely on a single
fixed development sequence.
3.2 Methodological Approach
EduVerse was developed using a hybrid iterative methodology with a mainly
feature-based vertical-slice approach. Development was organized around
individual academic and administrative features. Initial requirements were
identified primarily through the project team’s prior life experience with
educational and digital learning environments. Each feature was analyzed,
implemented across the required system layers, tested, and refined before
being integrated with the wider platform. This iterative process allowed
requirements and implementation details to be adjusted as development
progressed.
3.2.1 Iterative Feature-Centered Development
Development was organized around meaningful functional capabilities rather
than around isolated technical layers. Each iteration focused on a selected
academicoradministrativefeatureandmoveditthroughanalysis, interaction
design, implementation, testing, and integration.
This feature-centered organization kept development tied to recognizable
user or institutional outcomes while still allowing the required technical work
to span multiple system layers. One completed increment could also reveal
requirements or dependencies that informed the planning and refinement of
subsequent work.
The iterative process also supported coordination between the primary
web application and the mobile companion application. Features intended

Chapter 3. Methodology 17
for mobile use were refined across both applications, while more extensive
administrative and teaching workflows remained mainly on the web.
3.2.2 Vertical-Slice Realization
A feature was generally treated as a coherent functional unit rather than
divided into separate interface-only or backend-only development stages.
Depending on its scope, a feature slice could involve user interaction, business
rules, APIs, permissions, and persistent data.
For example, workflows such as assignment submission or examination
scheduling require more than an interface change because their behavior also
dependsontheactinguser, governingrules, andstoredacademicinformation.
The approach was predominantly, rather than exclusively, vertical.
Some features required changes across several system layers, while others
involved only a subset of those layers or extended into the mobile companion
application. The methodology therefore favored complete functional paths
where appropriate without requiring every increment to modify every layer
of the system.
3.2.3 Why This Methodology Fits EduVerse
A rigid sequential methodology was less suitable for EduVerse because many
platform capabilities share permissions, data, user context, and interaction
rules. Implementing and examining related functionality in practice clarified
these dependencies progressively.
An iterative approach allowed these dependencies to be addressed
progressively. Testing and refinement provided opportunities to identify
inconsistencies in workflows, permissions, interfaces, and data behavior
before each feature became fully integrated with the surrounding platform.
The vertical-slice emphasis complemented this iterative process by
keeping development focused on functional user outcomes rather than
isolated technical components. This was particularly useful in a multi-role
system where related workflows may behave differently for Organization
Administrators, Teachers, and Students.

3.3 Repeated Development Cycle
Each development increment followed a repeated six-stage cycle, with the
depth of each stage adjusted according to the feature and the system layers
involved. A relatively localized change could require limited supporting
work, while a broader feature might involve interface behavior, services,
permissions, persistent data, and mobile participation.
Regardless of scope, the same progression was maintained from feature
selection through analysis, design, implementation, testing, and final
integration into the wider platform.

3.4 Chapter Summary
EduVerse was developed using a hybrid iterative methodology that
combined feature-centered planning with predominantly vertical-slice
implementation. Development progressed through repeated cycles of feature
selection, workflow analysis, behavior and interaction design, feature-slice

present the resulting system analysis, design, implementation, and testing.

Chapter 3. Methodology 18
3.1 Introduction
Choosing a development methodology for EduVerse was not a routine
decision. The platform’s modules, including organization governance, class
operation, learning content, assessment, communication, AI support, and
integrated IDE support, are not independent; each depends on shared
permissions, shared data, and the roles of the Organization Administrator,
Teacher, and Student. A methodology that fixed requirements and structure
at the outset, before these dependencies were understood, risked producing
modules that worked in isolation but conflicted once integrated.
This chapter presents the methodological reasoning behind EduVerse’s
development: what approach was chosen, why it suited a multi-organization
educational platform, and how it was applied consistently across features.
Engineering practices and tool-specific execution are addressed separately in
Chapter 6.
3.2 System Development Methodology
EduVerse was developed using a hybrid iterative methodology with
predominantly feature-based vertical-slice development, rather than a
strict waterfall model in which analysis, design, implementation, and
validation each occur once in a fixed sequence. The platform instead evolved
through repeated increments, each centered on a meaningful academic or
administrative capability, allowing requirements and structure to be refined
as the relationships between modules became clearer through development.
3.2.1 Feature-Based Iterative Methodology
Development was organized around functional areas rather than technical
layers. Iterations typically focused on modules such as organization
management, class management, materials, assignments, examinations,
live sessions, results, AI Agent support, integrated IDE support, feature
configuration, and public access workflows. Within each iteration, the
selected feature moved through recurring stages of analysis, design,
development, and validation, with the outcome of one increment informing
the next.
This structure also governed coordination between the web application,

Chapter 3. Methodology 19
which served as the primary client, and the MVP mobile companion
application. Because the mobile app targeted selected high-frequency
academic actions rather than full feature parity, each iteration served as a
checkpoint for deciding which workflows required cross-client refinement and
which remained web-centered.
3.2.2 Vertical-Slice Development Approach
A feature was generally treated as a coherent functional unit rather than
split into isolated interface-only or backend-only stages. Depending on its
scope, a slice could span user-interface behavior, business rules, backend
or API behavior, permission handling, and data requirements. This suited
a role-based platform: an action such as submitting an assignment or
scheduling an examination cannot be understood as a user-interface concern
alone, since it also depends on who may perform it, what rules govern it,
and how the resulting record is stored and retrieved.
This description is deliberately framed as predominantly vertical-slice
rather than absolute. Some features required only a subset of system layers,
while others extended across several and, in selected cases, into the MVP
mobile companion application as well.
3.2.3 Justification for Methodology Selection
A rigid sequential methodology was a poor fit for EduVerse because the
platform’s module boundaries and dependencies were not fully knowable
in advance; they became clear through implementation. Organization
governance, class operation, learning content, assessment, communication,
AI support, and integrated IDE support influence one another through
shared permissions, shared data, and shared user context, so fixing their
design before that interplay was understood would have risked structural
rework later.
The iterative, vertical-slice approach let the project refine permissions,
workflows, interface behavior, and data structures incrementally, checking
after each increment whether a feature remained coherent with the wider
platform before expanding further. This mattered in particular because
the Organization Administrator, Teacher, and Student each interact with
related features from different perspectives, so role-based access and workflow
consistency needed repeated, not one-time, validation.

Chapter 3. Methodology 20
3.3 Iterative Development Structure
Although development was iterative, each increment followed the same
underlying cycle, adjusted in scope and depth to the complexity of the
feature involved. Some increments centered mainly on the web application;
others required supporting changes to the backend, database, permissions,
or MVP mobile companion application. What stayed constant was not
the shape of each iteration but the sequence it followed, moving from
clarification, through realization and validation, to integration.

where the platform’s structure and technical realization are presented in
greater detail.

Chapter 3. Methodology 17
3.1 Introduction
EduVerse combines interdependent workflows, roles, clients, services, and
configurable features that share data and access rules. Its methodology
therefore needed to support progressive refinement and controlled integration
as these dependencies became clearer during development. Methodology
choice was particularly important because access control, persistence, and
user interaction could not be refined independently without affecting the
coherence of the platform.
3.2 Methodological Approach
EduVerse was developed using a hybrid iterative methodology with
predominantly feature-based vertical-slice development, rather than a
strict waterfall model in which analysis, design, implementation, and
validation each occur once in a fixed sequence. The platform instead evolved
through repeated increments, each centered on a meaningful academic or
administrative capability, allowing requirements and structure to be refined
as the relationships between modules became clearer through development.
3.2.1 Iterative Feature-Centered Development
Development was organized around functional areas rather than technical
layers. Iterations focused on modules such as organization and class
management, materials, assessment, live sessions, results, AI Agent
and integrated IDE support, feature configuration, and public access.
Each selected feature moved through analysis, design, development, and
validation, with one increment informing the next. Organizing work in this
way kept each cycle tied to a recognizable user or institutional outcome
while allowing technical work to span the layers needed to deliver it.
The same iterations coordinated the primary web application with
the MVP mobile companion. They provided checkpoints for deciding
which high-frequency workflows required cross-client refinement and which
remained web-centered.

Chapter 3. Methodology 18
3.2.2 Vertical-Slice Realization
A feature was generally treated as a coherent functional unit rather than
split into interface-only or backend-only stages. Depending on scope, a slice
could span interface behavior, business rules, APIs, permissions, and data.
For example, assignment submission and examination scheduling depend on
the actor, governing rules, and persistence as well as the interface. The
approach was predominantly, not exclusively, vertical: some features required
only a subset of layers, while others also extended into the MVP mobile
companion. This qualification preserves an important distinction between
a methodological preference for complete feature paths and an inflexible
requirement that every increment modify every system layer.
3.2.3 Why This Methodology Fits EduVerse
A rigid sequential methodology was unsuitable because module boundaries
and dependencies became clearer through implementation. Organization
governance, class operation, assessment, communication, AI support, and the
integrated IDE share permissions, data, and user context; fixing their design
before examining that interplay would have increased the risk of rework.
Incremental checks allowed permissions, workflows, interfaces, and data
structures to be refined while remaining coherent with the wider platform.
Repeated validation was particularly important because the Organization
Administrator, Teacher, and Student interact with related features under
different access conditions, and some workflows span both web and mobile.
3.3 Repeated Development Cycle
Each increment followed the cycle in Table 3.1, with its depth adjusted to
the feature and the system layers involved. A web-centered change could
require limited supporting work, whereas another increment might extend
through the API, database, permissions, and mobile companion. In both
cases, the cycle retained the same progression from scope clarification to
platform integration.
Version control and pull-request review kept changes bounded to a feature
slice while supporting review of integration effects before merge.

Chapter 3. Methodology 18
3.1 Introduction
Choosing a development methodology for EduVerse was not a routine
decision. The platform’s modules, including organization governance, class
operation, learning content, assessment, communication, AI support, and
integrated IDE support, are not independent; each depends on shared
permissions, shared data, and the roles of the Organization Administrator,
Teacher, and Student. A methodology that fixed requirements and structure
at the outset, before these dependencies were understood, risked producing
modules that worked in isolation but conflicted once integrated.
This chapter presents the methodological reasoning behind EduVerse’s
development: what approach was chosen, why it suited a multi-organization
educational platform, and how it was applied consistently across features.
Engineering practices and tool-specific execution are addressed separately in
Chapter 6.
3.2 System Development Methodology
EduVerse was developed using a hybrid iterative methodology with
predominantly feature-based vertical-slice development, rather than a
strict waterfall model in which analysis, design, implementation, and
validation each occur once in a fixed sequence. The platform instead evolved
through repeated increments, each centered on a meaningful academic or
administrative capability, allowing requirements and structure to be refined
as the relationships between modules became clearer through development.
3.2.1 Feature-Based Iterative Methodology
Development was organized around functional areas rather than technical
layers. Iterations typically focused on modules such as organization
management, class management, materials, assignments, examinations,
live sessions, results, AI Agent support, integrated IDE support, feature
configuration, and public access workflows. Within each iteration, the
selected feature moved through recurring stages of analysis, design,
development, and validation, with the outcome of one increment informing
the next.
This structure also governed coordination between the web application,

Chapter 3. Methodology 19
which served as the primary client, and the MVP mobile companion
application. Because the mobile app targeted selected high-frequency
academic actions rather than full feature parity, each iteration served as a
checkpoint for deciding which workflows required cross-client refinement and
which remained web-centered.
3.2.2 Vertical-Slice Development Approach
A feature was generally treated as a coherent functional unit rather than
split into isolated interface-only or backend-only stages. Depending on its
scope, a slice could span user-interface behavior, business rules, backend
or API behavior, permission handling, and data requirements. This suited
a role-based platform: an action such as submitting an assignment or
scheduling an examination cannot be understood as a user-interface concern
alone, since it also depends on who may perform it, what rules govern it,
and how the resulting record is stored and retrieved.
This description is deliberately framed as predominantly vertical-slice
rather than absolute. Some features required only a subset of system layers,
while others extended across several and, in selected cases, into the MVP
mobile companion application as well.
3.2.3 Justification for Methodology Selection
A rigid sequential methodology was a poor fit for EduVerse because the
platform’s module boundaries and dependencies were not fully knowable
in advance; they became clear through implementation. Organization
governance, class operation, learning content, assessment, communication,
AI support, and integrated IDE support influence one another through
shared permissions, shared data, and shared user context, so fixing their
design before that interplay was understood would have risked structural
rework later.
The iterative, vertical-slice approach let the project refine permissions,
workflows, interface behavior, and data structures incrementally, checking
after each increment whether a feature remained coherent with the wider
platform before expanding further. This mattered in particular because
the Organization Administrator, Teacher, and Student each interact with
related features from different perspectives, so role-based access and workflow
consistency needed repeated, not one-time, validation.

Chapter 3. Methodology 16
3.1 Introduction
EduVerse combines multiple academic and administrative workflows that
share user roles, data, permissions, and interaction rules. Developing these
capabilities therefore required a methodology that could accommodate
progressive refinement while preserving consistency across the wider
platform.
Because dependencies between features often became clearer during
implementation and testing, the development process needed to support
repeated analysis, refinement, and integration rather than rely on a single
fixed development sequence.
3.2 Methodological Approach
EduVerse was developed using a hybrid iterative methodology with a mainly
feature-based vertical-slice approach. Development was organized around
individual academic and administrative features. Initial requirements were
identified primarily through the project team’s prior life experience with
educational and digital learning environments. Each feature was analyzed,
implemented across the required system layers, tested, and refined before
being integrated with the wider platform. This iterative process allowed
requirements and implementation details to be adjusted as development
progressed.
3.2.1 Iterative Feature-Centered Development
Development was organized around meaningful functional capabilities rather
than around isolated technical layers. Each iteration focused on a selected
academicoradministrativefeatureandmoveditthroughanalysis, interaction
design, implementation, testing, and integration.
This feature-centered organization kept development tied to recognizable
user or institutional outcomes while still allowing the required technical work
to span multiple system layers. One completed increment could also reveal
requirements or dependencies that informed the planning and refinement of
subsequent work.
The iterative process also supported coordination between the primary
web application and the mobile companion application. Features intended

Chapter 3. Methodology 17
for mobile use were refined across both applications, while more extensive
administrative and teaching workflows remained mainly on the web.
3.2.2 Vertical-Slice Realization
A feature was generally treated as a coherent functional unit rather than
divided into separate interface-only or backend-only development stages.
Depending on its scope, a feature slice could involve user interaction, business
rules, APIs, permissions, and persistent data.
For example, workflows such as assignment submission or examination
scheduling require more than an interface change because their behavior also
dependsontheactinguser, governingrules, andstoredacademicinformation.
The approach was predominantly, rather than exclusively, vertical.
Some features required changes across several system layers, while others
involved only a subset of those layers or extended into the mobile companion
application. The methodology therefore favored complete functional paths
where appropriate without requiring every increment to modify every layer
of the system.
3.2.3 Why This Methodology Fits EduVerse
A rigid sequential methodology was less suitable for EduVerse because many
platform capabilities share permissions, data, user context, and interaction
rules. Implementing and examining related functionality in practice clarified
these dependencies progressively.
An iterative approach allowed these dependencies to be addressed
progressively. Testing and refinement provided opportunities to identify
inconsistencies in workflows, permissions, interfaces, and data behavior
before each feature became fully integrated with the surrounding platform.
The vertical-slice emphasis complemented this iterative process by
keeping development focused on functional user outcomes rather than
isolated technical components. This was particularly useful in a multi-role
system where related workflows may behave differently for Organization
Administrators, Teachers, and Students.

3.4 Chapter Summary
EduVerse was developed using a hybrid iterative methodology that
combined feature-centered planning with predominantly vertical-slice
implementation. Development progressed through repeated cycles of feature
selection, workflow analysis, behavior and interaction design, feature-slice
implementation, testing and refinement, and platform integration. This
approach supported progressive refinement while preserving coherence across
related academic and administrative workflows. The following chapters
present the resulting system analysis, design, implementation, and testing.
